executive_summary: Green hydrogen electrolyzers face a fundamental demand problem despite improving technology and generous tax incentives. The 2027 construction deadline for Section 45V eligibility creates a narrow window, but 90% of announced capacity lacks identified buyers, real-world electrolyzer costs remain 60-300% above published assumptions, and major incumbents like BP and Air Products are canceling projects. The sector is not investable at scale today. Monitor technology plays like Hysata for 12-18 months while the demand picture clarifies, with the risk that the 2027 deadline passes before viable offtake materializes.

market_shifts.description: Final rules for the Section 45V Clean Hydrogen Production Tax Credit were released on January 3, 2025, offering up to $3.00 per kilogram of clean hydrogen as a 10-year incentive, but eligibility was restricted in mid-2025 to facilities beginning construction before the end of 2027.

Multiple large-scale hydrogen projects were cancelled between December 2025 and February 2025, including BP's 1.5 GW Duqm project in Oman (150,000 tonnes annually) and Air Products' $500 million Massena plant (35 tons per day), driven by regulatory changes rendering existing power supplies ineligible for tax credits, elevated production costs, and weak demand.

Three large green hydrogen projects reached Final Investment Decision in 2026: Orica's 50 MW Hunter Valley Hub (the largest Australian renewable hydrogen project to reach FID), the 30 MW Barrow Green Hydrogen Project, and Hy2gen's 275 MW Courant decarbonized ammonium nitrate project.

The first long-term green hydrogen offtake agreement of scale was signed on March 12, 2025, when RWE and TotalEnergies committed to a 15-year contract for approximately 30,000 metric tons per year for TotalEnergies' Leuna refinery, even as only 10% of globally announced projects have identified buyers.

Real-world 2024 electrolyzer system costs averaged $3,000/kW, 60% to 300% higher than previously cited assumptions of $1,800/kW, while PEM electrolyzer CAPEX fell from roughly $1,200-$1,500 per kW in 2020 to approximately $700-$1,000 per kW by 2026.

U.S. Department of Energy awarded $34 million in tax credits to John Cockerill Hydrogen's Baytown Gigafactory in Texas, expected to produce 1 GW per year of alkaline electrolyzer manufacturing capacity and create 200 jobs, marking a major incumbent's expansion into U.S. manufacturing.

recommendations.text: Track Hysata's commercialization progress for 12-18 months given its peer-reviewed 95% efficiency achievement versus 75% for commercial alternatives, representing a 20-percentage-point improvement that could materially alter project economics if it scales. The risk is that superior technology proves irrelevant if offtake demand remains weak and the 2027 construction deadline for Section 45V eligibility expires before projects can secure buyers.

Watch whether the three 2026 Final Investment Decision projects—Orica's 50 MW Hunter Valley Hub, the 30 MW Barrow project, and Hy2gen's 275 MW Courant facility—reach commercial operation and demonstrate viable unit economics by mid-2027. These are the first projects of scale to clear FID in the current regulatory environment. The risk is capital-intensity: real-world electrolyzer costs average $3,000/kW, not the $1,800/kW assumption most models use, meaning these projects may still fail to prove commercial viability even with tax credits.

Pass on electrolyzer manufacturing or project development plays until demand fundamentals improve. Only 10% of announced global capacity has identified buyers, BP canceled a 150,000 tonne-per-year project in December 2025, and Air Products exited a $500 million plant in February 2025 after regulatory changes. The RWE-TotalEnergies 30,000 tonne-per-year offtake agreement is the lone bright spot in a market where developers are broadly scaling back due to weak demand and elevated costs. The regulatory risk is timeline: the 2027 construction deadline for Section 45V means projects that cannot secure offtake in the next 12 months lose their primary subsidy, and there is no evidence the offtake gap is closing at the required pace.

Source deals in green hydrogen end-use applications—particularly industrial buyers with existing gray hydrogen consumption like refineries or ammonia producers—rather than electrolyzer technology or project developers. The TotalEnergies 15-year offtake for 30,000 tonnes annually at its Leuna refinery demonstrates that offtake is the binding constraint, not technology or subsidy availability. The risk is that even industrial users with clear decarbonization mandates prove unwilling to pay the premium for green hydrogen at scale, but this is a lower-risk entry point than manufacturing or project development given capital requirements.

all_claims.claim: Electric Hydrogen (EH2) raised $380 million in an oversubscribed Series C round announced October 3, 2023, bringing its total funding to roughly $600 million.
As of a July 2026 company profile, Electric Hydrogen has raised $603M in total funding from investors including Energy Impact Partners, Fifth Wall, and Fortescue.
Green hydrogen startup Hysata raised $111 million in a Series B round announced May 9, 2024.
Hysata's capillary-fed electrolyser (CFE) technology has achieved 95% system efficiency, confirmed at commercial scale, versus roughly 75% efficiency for existing commercial electrolysers.
A peer-reviewed 2022 Nature Communications paper reported Hysata's capillary-fed electrolysis cell achieving 95% (HHV) energy efficiency at 0.8 A/cm² and 85°C, equating to 39.4–41.6 kWh per kg of H2.
John Cockerill Hydrogen entered the U.S. market by acquiring manufacturing space in Baytown, Texas to build a new electrolyzer gigafactory.

John Cockerill Hydrogen was awarded $34 million in U.S. Department of Energy tax credits for its Baytown Gigafactory project, out of $42 billion in total funding requests submitted for that DOE allocation round.
The Baytown, Texas John Cockerill facility is expected to create 200 new jobs and produce 1 GW per year of alkaline electrolyzer manufacturing capacity.
The U.S. Treasury and IRS released final rules for the Section 45V Clean Hydrogen Production Tax Credit on January 3, 2025, offering up to $3.00 per kilogram of clean hydrogen as a 10-year incentive.
Under a revised U.S. law passed in mid-2025, only clean hydrogen facilities that begin construction before the end of 2027 remain eligible to receive the Section 45V tax credit.
The U.S. DOE's technical target for PEM electrolysis is $2/kg for clean hydrogen production by 2026, with a longer-term goal of $1/kg by 2031.
PEM electrolyzer CAPEX fell from roughly $1,200–$1,500 per kW in 2020 to approximately $700–$1,000 per kW by 2026, according to H2Pro.

A 2024 industry review (cited via LinkedIn analysis of Fletcher's data) found real-world 2024 electrolyzer system costs averaging $3,000/kW, far higher than a commonly cited CSIRO assumption of $1,800/kW — indicating electrolysis costs have historically been underestimated by 60% to 300%.

RWE and TotalEnergies signed a long-term (15-year) offtake agreement announced March 12, 2025, under which TotalEnergies will purchase approximately 30,000 metric tons of green hydrogen per year from RWE for its Leuna, Germany refinery.

Plug Power was selected in April 2026 to supply a 275 MW GenEco electrolyzer system under a Front-End Engineering Design (FEED) contract for Hy2gen's Courant decarbonized ammonium nitrate project in Baie-Comeau, Québec, Canada.

Plug Power won a 50 MW electrolyzer order (announced July 7, 2026) as Orica's Hunter Valley Hub in Australia became the largest Australian renewable hydrogen project to reach Final Investment Decision.
The 30 MW Barrow Green Hydrogen Project reached Final Investment Decision on May 20, 2026, with Plug Power supplying 30 MW of its GenEco PEM electrolyzers.
As of September 2024, 255 hydrogen project developers were actively negotiating offtake agreements with buyers or had already signed them, per Wood Mackenzie.

Of all clean hydrogen production capacity planned globally by 2030, only about 10% of announced projects have identified a buyer, according to BloombergNEF research cited by the Green Hydrogen Organisation.

Air Products announced on February 24, 2025 that it would exit three U.S.-based projects, including canceling its planned $500 million liquid green hydrogen plant in Massena, New York, because recent regulatory developments rendered its existing hydroelectric power supply ineligible for the hydrogen production tax credit.
The Massena, New York plant that Air Products cancelled was designed to produce 35 tons per day of green hydrogen.
BP cancelled the gigascale 1.5 GW Duqm Green Hydrogen Project in Oman in December 2025, which had been designed to produce 150,000 tonnes of hydrogen annually.
Developers of green hydrogen projects have scaled back investments and scrapped projects globally due to elevated production costs and weak demand, according to Reuters reporting from July 23, 2025.
